title: Why does the AI game dev community do not create an AI-oriented engine?
author: Nearby_Ad4786
selftext:
I follow this forum just as curiosity. It's incredible the number of people working in parallel on "I made this game from scratch using 31233M of tokens".

What about if we start a collaboration on a game engine oriented to work with an AI agent? As an amateur game dev, I think that it is stupid to start from 0 any time that you work on a project. I wouldn't create a library of physics or animations having Unity, Godot, Blender...

What do you think?

comments.author: ZedIsAPrimeNumber
comments.body: What do you mean with engine? what's wrong with Godot or Unity? What would a dedicated engine solve? You can always ask for a game in any language.

replies.author: silly_bet_3454
replies.body:
Even though I totally agree with you and this is the best answer, I also have to admit I've considered trying to make an AI engine too. The specific purpose would be to cater to the true noobs who have no experience with any dev or game dev. Of course today for professionals and experienced devs you can integrate with current engines, but imagine an "AI first" engine where the main interface is just simply a chat, integrated into the UI. Everything in the engine is designed to be simple and scriptable from the start and basically just tuned for AI workflows specifically.

I researched this idea at one point and my impression is that Roblox has something like this but I'm not sure.

replies.author: The_R1NG
replies.body:
You’re not bringing new information, you stated you are new to development yet you have an attitude like you actually grasp what you’re talking about at a deeper level than others which I find bemusing but not surprising.

In short it’s because it’s a dumb idea, AI works with engines that exist, are already built, have teams and funding behind them and massive communities already entrenched. 

If a developer is using AI and no engine then they wouldn’t use an AI engine, if they can articulate why they would then they could find an existing engine that works. 

There is no need for people to build an engine for an ever evolving tool with regulations etc changing and in the horizon instead of utilizing that tool to build on an engine that’s proven by time.

replies.author: joran213
replies.body: There could be two reasons why people do that. They either don't know ai works better with a game engine, or they just don't care and are too lazy. A new ai game engine wouldn't work in both of those cases. If people don't know about the most popular game engines, they're not suddenly gonna become aware of this new ai game engine (at least not without massive marketing or word of mouth). And people too lazy to leave the claude interface are likely also going to be too lazy to use any kind of engine, ai focused or not.

Ok? This is a 7+ year old project. Before LLMs. I'm aware of the concept of reusable libraries.

comments.author: Rensuto
comments.body:
I'm personally working on an engine + editor alongside my game. I find that a lot of the engines do not have the plug-ins I seek or not in the way I'd prefer it done. Mine is writilen in c# for scripting layer, c++ for graphics layer. 
Unlike most engines, I have full sprite generator for 2d games utilizing a custom harness, same for 3d model gen utilizing api'd applications, similar to what you'd find in meshy or pixel lab.

I'd be going in circles, but your own engine will never hurt and likely make it easier for long term support. To also mention, in the process of building your own engine, you will by consequence, design a coherent game using those systems.

Id be down to give you a demo or just bounce ideas.

comments.author: LordKwik
comments.body:
I hear you. 

I got into game dev a few years ago with a few coworkers: two artists and a programmer, with me as the product manager. I signed us up for a game jam, and things were looking good. we started with Godot, then the programmer wanted to learn Unity instead, but it was a bit late to switch, so me and one artist started helping him out in Godot. I went to school for IT, and my jobs have required me to work in XML, HTML, and SQL, so while I'm not scared of any language, I'm not exactly proficient in any one of them. the team eventually fell apart due to life events, and as far as I know, only me and the 3D artist are working on solo projects, both using AI. he's already made a demo for his wife, and I have a few prototypes in the works. 

so now, when I'm planning out a game and everything I want in it, one of the questions I ask chatGPT/Codex is "what is the best engine to use for this project?" and while I tried to do my own research and dig deeper into what might actually be best, I don't really know and kinda have to take its word for it. so yeah, a solid starting point would be really nice for someone who doesn't exactly know what they're doing, just knows what they want out of it. I'm willing to learn of course, but the willingness alone isn't a guarantee for success. I've run into some issues that others have as well, and have to ask Codex to simplify the code or make it run better or whatever, and yeah it's just not efficient. 

I don't really know what it takes to achieve what you're asking for, but I feel like it would benefit someone like me 🤷‍♂️

comments.author: owenwp
comments.body:
What would such an engine do that Unreal/Unity/Godot do not already do? 

  
Also, making something from scratch is usually less total work than trying to modify something that already exists, even if humans find the latter easier to wrap their heads around. AI doesn't care that starting over means lots of boilerplate and boring low level systems work. It doesn't need to jump right to the creative work in order to be engaged and productive. All of the things that intimidate indie game devs into stalling out don't matter to Claude.

comments.author: sirpalee
comments.body:
Because nowadays it can be quicker to wire together an "engine" for your specific game rather than trying to fit (a small) game idea into an established engine. Since you have all the source, the agent knows what's going on.

Game engines take a lot of time (tokens) to be built, and seeing how fast the ai space is moving, your approaches could be outdated by the time you have an MVP. CLI/MCP access to established/battle tested engines sounds a better ROI. Like what unity is doing with unity cli.
